steps.title: Word Order — SOV
steps.body: Korean follows Subject → Object → Verb (SOV) order. The verb always comes LAST.
rules: Korean (SOV): 나는 밥을 먹어요. (I rice eat.)
Tip: Listen for the final word — that's the verb, the action!

tip.label: Grammar Tip
tip.text: Once you know the verb comes last, everything clicks. The rest of the sentence can rearrange — Korean speakers use particles to keep things clear.

steps.meaning_ja: 私はご飯を食べます。（主語＋目的語＋動詞）
steps.katakana: ナヌン パブル モゴヨ

steps.prompt: In a Korean sentence, the verb always comes...

steps.title: Korean Particles
steps.body: Particles attach to nouns to show their role: topic, subject, object, location. They replace fixed word order.
rules: 은/는 → Topic marker (은 after consonant, 는 after vowel)
이/가 → Subject marker (이 after consonant, 가 after vowel)
을/를 → Object marker (을 after consonant, 를 after vowel)

steps.meaning: I am a student. (는 = topic marker)
steps.meaning_ja: 私は学生です。（는 = トピックマーカー）
steps.katakana: ナヌン ハクセンイエヨ

steps.meaning: Rain comes. / It's raining. (가 = subject marker)
steps.meaning_ja: 雨が来ます。（雨が降っています）（가 = 主語マーカー）

steps.prompt: To mark 밥 (rice) as the OBJECT: 밥___ 먹어요

steps.meaning: I drink coffee at the café. (에서 = location of action)
steps.meaning_ja: カフェでコーヒーを飲みます。（에서 = 動作の場所）
steps.katakana: カペエソ コピルル マショヨ

steps.title: Verbs — Dictionary Form
steps.body: All Korean verbs in dictionary form end in 다 (da). Remove 다 to get the verb stem, then add an ending.

steps.title: Present Tense: -아요 / -어요
steps.body: Add -아요 after ㅏ or ㅗ stems. Add -어요 for all others. 하다 verbs use -해요.

tip.label: Vowel Rule
tip.text: ㅏ and ㅗ are 'bright' vowels → -아요. All other vowels are 'dark' → -어요. Once you know the stem vowel, conjugation is automatic.

steps.meaning: I go / Let's go. (가다 → 가요, polite present)
steps.meaning_ja: 行きます / 行きましょう。（가다 → 가요、丁寧な現在形）

steps.meaning: I eat / eating. (먹다 → 먹어요, polite present)
steps.meaning_ja: 食べます。（먹다 → 먹어요、丁寧な現在形）

steps.title: Past Tense: -았어요 / -었어요
steps.body: Add -았어요 after ㅏ/ㅗ stems and -었어요 for others. 하다 → 했어요.

steps.title: Future Tense: -(으)ㄹ 거예요
steps.body: Add -(으)ㄹ 거예요 to the verb stem to talk about future plans or predictions.

steps.title: Making Sentences Negative
steps.body: Short negation: 안 + verb. Long negation: verb stem + 지 않아요. Cannot: 못 + verb.

steps.title: Forming Questions
steps.body: Korean questions use the SAME word order as statements — just add rising intonation (↑) or a question mark.

tip.label: Grammar Tip
tip.text: 밥을 먹어요 = I eat rice. 밥을 먹어요? = Do you eat rice? Same words — just a rising tone at the end. No word inversion like English!

steps.katakana: イルミ ムォイェヨ？

steps.title: Essential Sentence Patterns
steps.body: Master these 6 patterns to express the most common ideas in Korean conversations.
rules: ~고 싶어요 — want to: 한국에 가고 싶어요 (I want to go to Korea)
~ㄹ/을 수 있어요 — can: 한국어를 할 수 있어요 (I can speak Korean)
~아/어야 해요 — must: 공부해야 해요 (I must study)
~(으)면 — if/when: 비가 오면 집에 있어요 (If it rains, I stay home)
~때문에 — because of: 비 때문에 못 가요 (Can't go because of rain)

steps.prompt: Pattern for 'I want to go to Korea': 한국에 ___

steps.title: Connectors
steps.body: These 4 conjunctions connect sentences. Place them at the START of the second sentence.
rules: 그리고 — And / And then (adds information or sequence)
그런데 — But / By the way (soft contrast, casual — most common!)

tip.label: Usage Tip
tip.text: 그런데 is one of the most common words in spoken Korean — it softens contrast and shifts topics smoothly. 그렇지만 is stronger and more formal.

steps.meaning: It rained. So I stayed home.
steps.meaning_ja: 雨が降りました。だから家にいました。
steps.katakana: ピガ ワッソヨ。クレソ チベ イッソッソヨ。

steps.prompt: Soft contrast or topic shift — most common in spoken Korean?

steps.title: And, With
steps.body: Use these particles between nouns (not sentences) to mean 'and' or 'with'.
rules: -하고 — after any noun, neutral/casual: 친구하고 갔어요 (went with a friend)
-(이)랑 — 이랑 (consonant) / 랑 (vowel), very casual: 오빠랑 놀았어요 (played with older brother)
-와/과 — 와 (vowel) / 과 (consonant), formal/written: 선생님과 상담했어요 (consulted with teacher)

steps.title: To/From Someone
steps.body: Use person-directional particles when giving to or receiving from people, not places.
rules: -한테 — to (a person): 친구한테 전화했어요 (called my friend)
-한테서 — from (a person): 선생님한테서 배웠어요 (learned from teacher)

steps.title: Telling Time
steps.body: Use NATIVE Korean numbers for hours (시) and SINO-KOREAN numbers for minutes (분). AM = 오전, PM = 오후.
rules: Half past: 반 — 세 시 반 = 3:30
Example: 오후 두 시 삼십 분 = 2:30 PM

tip.label: Key Pattern
tip.text: Hours use Native Korean numbers (한, 두, 세...). Minutes use Sino-Korean numbers (일, 이, 삼...). Half past = 반. AM = 오전, PM = 오후.

steps.katakana: チグム ミョッ シイェヨ？

steps.prompt: Hours in Korean time use which number system?

steps.title: Counters
steps.body: Korean uses specific counters after [Noun] + [Number]. Native Korean numbers (한, 두, 세...) are used with most counters.
rules: 개 — general objects: 사과 세 개 (3 apples)
명 — people (neutral): 학생 두 명 (2 students)
분 — people (honorific): 손님 두 분 (2 guests)
마리 — animals: 고양이 한 마리 (1 cat)
권 — books: 책 세 권 (3 books)
잔 — cups/drinks: 커피 두 잔 (2 coffees)

steps.katakana: サグァ セ ゲ チュセヨ

steps.title: Present Progressive
steps.body: Add -고 있어요 to the verb stem to say someone IS CURRENTLY doing something (the Korean '-ing' form).

tip.label: Progressive vs Simple
tip.text: 먹어요 = I eat (general or right now, context-dependent). 먹고 있어요 = I am eating (specifically in progress at this moment). The progressive adds 'currently in action.'

steps.meaning_ja: 今、ご飯を食べています。
steps.katakana: チグム パブル モッコ イッソヨ

steps.title: Self Introduction
steps.body: Key vocabulary: 이름 (name), 나이 (age), 나라 (country), 직업 (job), 취미 (hobby), 고향 (hometown).

tip.label: Template
tip.text: Use 안녕하세요 + 잘 부탁드려요 for formal settings. With friends or peers: 안녕! + 잘 부탁해! Always bow slightly when introducing yourself in person.

steps.title: Dates and Months
steps.body: Korean dates use Sino-Korean numbers in Year → Month → Day order. June = 유월, October = 시월 (exceptions).
rules: 일월(1월), 이월(2월), 삼월(3월), 사월(4월), 오월(5월), 유월(6월)
칠월(7월), 팔월(8월), 구월(9월), 시월(10월), 십일월(11월), 십이월(12월)
오늘이 며칠이에요? — What is today's date?

steps.title: Degree Adverbs
steps.body: Degree adverbs go directly before the word they modify: 조금 (a little), 정말 (really), 아주 (very), 많이 (a lot).
rules: 조금 / 좀 — a little (좀 is softer/casual)
별로 + negative — not really (별로 안 좋아요 = I don't really like it)
전혀 + negative — not at all (전혀 모르겠어요 = I have no idea at all)

tip.label: Negative Adverbs
tip.text: 별로 and 전혀 MUST be used with a negative verb (안, 못, 없다, 모르다). Saying 별로 좋아요 (without negation) is ungrammatical. Think of them as 'not really' and 'not at all'.

steps.katakana: チョンマル マシッソヨ

steps.prompt: 별로 and 전혀 must be used with...

steps.title: Nominalizer: -는 것
steps.body: Adding -는 것 to a verb stem creates a noun phrase — 'the act of doing ~'. It makes verbs act like nouns.
rules: 먹는 것 — the act of eating
배우는 것 — the act of learning
한국어를 배우는 것이 재미있어요 — Learning Korean is interesting
요리하는 것을 좋아해요 — I like cooking (the act of cooking)

tip.label: Tense Forms
tip.text: -는 것 (present/habitual) · -(으)ㄴ 것 (past/completed) · -(으)ㄹ 것 (future/planned). The present form is the most common in daily speech.

steps.meaning_ja: 韓国語を学ぶことは面白いです。
steps.katakana: ハングゴルル ペウヌン ゴシ チェミイッソヨ

steps.title: Comparatives
steps.body: Structure: [A]이/가 [B]보다 더 [adjective]. 보다 means 'than' and 더 means 'more'.
rules: 한국어가 영어보다 더 어려워요 — Korean is harder than English
오늘이 어제보다 더 더워요 — Today is hotter than yesterday
더 can be dropped in casual speech: 한국어가 영어보다 어려워요

steps.meaning_ja: 韓国語は日本語より難しいです。
steps.katakana: ハングゴガ イルボノボダ オリョウォヨ

steps.prompt: How to say 'more' in a Korean comparison?

steps.title: 좋다 vs 좋아하다
steps.body: 좋다 uses subject particle (이/가): 한국어가 좋아요. 좋아하다 uses object particle (을/를): 한국어를 좋아해요.
rules: 좋다 — to be good / feel good (state): 커피가 좋아요 (I like coffee / Coffee is good)
좋아하다 — to like (active preference): 커피를 좋아해요 (I like coffee)
Both translate as 'I like' but 좋다 focuses on the feeling, 좋아하다 on the preference

tip.label: Key Difference
tip.text: 좋아요 → subject particle (이/가) precedes it. 좋아해요 → object particle (을/를) precedes it. When in doubt, 좋아해요 sounds more natural for expressing preferences.

steps.title: Still & Already
steps.body: 아직 + negative verb = still not. 벌써 = already (sooner than expected). 이미 = already (neutral, formal).
rules: 아직 안 먹었어요 — Haven't eaten yet (still not)

steps.title: Someone, Something
steps.body: Combine question words with context to express indefinite ideas like 'someone' or 'nothing'.
rules: 무언가 / 뭔가 — something: 뭔가 이상해요 (Something is strange)
아무도 + negative — no one: 아무도 없어요 (No one is here)
아무것도 + negative — nothing: 아무것도 몰라요 (I know nothing)

steps.title: Imperative: -(으)세요
steps.body: Add -(으)세요 to a verb stem to make a polite request or command.

steps.title: Don't: -지 마세요
steps.body: Add -지 마세요 to a verb stem to politely tell someone NOT to do something.

steps.meaning_ja: ゆっくり話してください。
steps.katakana: チョンチョニ マレ チュセヨ

steps.title: Method: -(으)로
steps.body: -(으)로 marks method or means — 'by' or 'with' a tool/way of doing something.
rules: -(으)로 after consonant, -로 after vowel: 버스로 가요 (go by bus)

steps.title: Good/Poor At
steps.body: 잘하다 = good at. 못하다 = poor at. Both attach after the object particle 을/를.
rules: 수영을 잘 못해요 (not very good at swimming)

steps.title: All, More: 다, 더
steps.body: 다 = all/everything. 더 = more. Both are simple adverbs placed before the verb.
rules: 다 먹었어요 — ate everything / all of it
다 더 다르게 쓰여요 — both are used very differently in context

steps.title: All, More & -도
steps.body: -도 has 4 advanced uses beyond simple 'also': emphasis, emphatic negation, and 'both...and'.
rules: 아이도 알아요 — even children know (emphasis: unexpected inclusion)
하나도 없어요 — not even one (emphatic negation: 하나도 + negative)
먹기도 해요 — sometimes eats / also eats (-기도 하다)
좋기도 하고 나쁘기도 해요 — both good and bad

steps.meaning: Korean is both difficult and interesting.
steps.meaning_ja: 韓国語は難しくもあり、面白くもあります。
steps.katakana: ハングゴガ オリョッキド ハゴ チェミイッキド ヘヨ

steps.title: Grammar Complete!
steps.message: You've mastered all 26 grammar stages — from SOV word order and particles to advanced -도 patterns. Start applying these in real conversations!
